name: Obsidian
tagline: Local-first Markdown knowledge base with backlinks, a graph view, and community plugins.
description: Obsidian stores notes as plain Markdown files on your own device, linked by backlinks and a graph, with community plugins and no required cloud.
pros: Notes are plain Markdown files on the user's device, so the library is readable and movable without the vendor
Bidirectional linking creates a graph view that reveals connections folder-based organization hides, per the note-taking comparison held in this repository
A community plugin marketplace extends the core app, so capability arrives without waiting on the vendor's roadmap
Local files can sit under git-based version control, a fit the developer guide in this repository calls out explicitly
Rated 4.6 out of 5 from 2,080 reviews in this repository's recorded data
cons: Local-first is single-player by default: real-time editing, shared workspaces, and team permissions are the axis the Notion-versus-Obsidian pages in this repository are written around
Community plugins mean vault behavior can depend on third-party code of uneven quality, with upkeep falling on whoever installed it
The app is recorded as free while sync and publish are paid additions, so multi-device convenience is not part of the free tier

content.title: Plain files in a folder on your disk
content.body: Obsidian's storage model is the product. Notes are Markdown files sitting in a folder on the user's device, which this repository records as the defining property of the app alongside privacy, longevity, and extensibility. Nothing has to be uploaded for the tool to work, and the folder stays readable in any editor if the application disappears. The developer-productivity guide in this repository draws the contrast directly: a file-based approach where notes are local Markdown, against a structured database approach where notes are rows in someone else's system.

content.title: Backlinks, the graph, and how notes connect
content.body: Because files can reference each other freely, the collection becomes a network rather than a filing tree. This repository records bidirectional linking in Obsidian as creating a knowledge graph, with a graph view showing connections that folder-based organization hides. Practically, a note can point at another and be found from it without either being filed anywhere; a topic page grows by accumulating links instead of being moved between folders. The knowledge-management material held here positions that as the reason to choose a local vault over a database.

content.title: Community plugins and what they add
content.body: Extensibility is recorded as one of Obsidian's value propositions, and it runs through a marketplace of community-developed plugins. The practical effect is that the core app stays small while capability is added by whoever maintains a plugin, which is also where the trade-off lives: plugin quality is uneven, upkeep falls on the person who installed it, and a vault's behavior can end up depending on third-party code. The surfaces below sit alongside that marketplace in the recorded feature set.

content.title: Version control over your own notes
content.body: Local files open an option the hosted note tools do not: the developer-productivity guide in this repository notes that Obsidian's file-based approach suits developers who prefer local Markdown with git-based version control. A vault can be committed, branched, and diffed like source, which turns note history into something reviewable and makes backups a copy operation rather than a vendor export. The same property pushes care onto the user, because a folder of files is only as safe as the machine and the backup routine behind it.

content.title: What a local vault does not give you
content.body: A local-first app is single-player by default. Real-time editing across a team, shared workspaces, and the permission model that comes with them are the axis the Notion-versus-Obsidian pages in this repository are written around, which tells a buyer where to look: collaboration features, pricing for ten or more users, real-time editing, and migration paths. Obsidian suits individuals and quiet small groups more than departments that need documents co-edited live. Teams that need that should read the Notion pages in this repository instead.

content.title: Free app, paid sync and publish
content.body: This page records Obsidian as free, and that is the only price statement here. The note-taking comparison in this repository adds the shape behind it: the application is free for personal use, while paid plans provide sync across devices, publish functionality, and commercial licensing. Because the notes already live on disk, sync is an optional convenience rather than the way the product works, which is unusual in this category and worth weighing against a tool whose data exists only on a vendor's servers.

content.title: What this repository does not record about security
content.body: Obsidian's local model answers part of the security question structurally: content sits on the user's device, so exposure depends on the device, its backups, and whatever sync the user switches on. The material collected for this page lists no compliance certification for Obsidian and no such assertion appears here; organizations that need a documented record work from the vendor’s published documentation rather than from this page. The practical questions for a team are different ones, namely how plugin code is vetted, where synced copies live, and who owns the vault when a contributor leaves.

content.title: Obsidian next to Notion, Roam, and Evernote
content.body: Notion is compared with Obsidian on two separate pages in this repository, both written around collaboration, shared workspaces, and migration, which is where the two tools actually diverge. Roam Research is the closer cousin in idea: linked notes, but hosted and outliner-shaped rather than a folder of files. Evernote is the capture-and-search store filed on the opposite side of the same category.

content.title: Who should keep a vault
content.body: Obsidian fits writers, developers, and researchers who want their notes to outlive the application that made them, and who are comfortable owning files rather than renting a workspace. It fits privacy-conscious users who would rather keep material on their own machine, and individuals who want a graph of links without a subscription. It does not fit departments that need live co-editing and permissions out of the box, or buyers who want a vendor-held compliance record on file. The reading above comes from this repository's stored records and the product's published material, not from any session spent using Obsidian. Those records show 4.6 out of 5 from 2,080 reviews.

faqs.question: Where are my notes stored with Obsidian?
faqs.answer: On your device, as plain Markdown files in a folder. This repository records local-first storage as the defining property of the app, alongside privacy, longevity, and extensibility.

faqs.question: Is Obsidian free?
faqs.answer: This page records it as free. The note-taking comparison in this repository adds that the application is free for personal use, while paid plans provide device sync, publishing, and commercial licensing.

faqs.question: Does Obsidian have a graph?
faqs.answer: Yes. This repository records bidirectional linking as creating a knowledge graph, with a graph view showing connections that traditional folder-based organization hides.

faqs.question: How does Obsidian differ from Roam Research?
faqs.answer: Both link notes bidirectionally. Roam is an outliner with daily notes and block references in a hosted service; Obsidian edits a folder of Markdown files stored on your own machine.

faqs.question: Can a team share an Obsidian vault?
faqs.answer: The Notion-versus-Obsidian pages in this repository are written around collaboration, real-time editing, shared workspaces, and migration, which is where a team buyer should look before committing.

author: Sarah Chen
learningCurve: Low to start writing, higher to design: links, plugins, and folder conventions need decisions before a vault is pleasant to live in
whoShouldUse: Writers, developers, researchers, and privacy-conscious individuals who want notes as local files, links instead of folders, and the option to extend the application with community plugins.
whoShouldNotUse: Departments that need real-time co-editing, shared workspaces, and permissions out of the box; teams that require a vendor-held compliance record; buyers who want sync included with the free tier.
